source_text:
Fragmenta in epistulam ad Philippenses (in catenis)
Phil: Prolog
̓Εν ταύτῃ τῇ ἐπιστολῇ κληρικοῖς γράφει οὐ λαϊκοῖς· δι' οπερ οὐδὲ πλειόνων ἐδεήθη
ἠδικῶν, σπουδὴ δὲ αὐτῷ διὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς τὸ τῆς ταπεινοφροσύνης κατορθωθῆναι
ἐν αὐτοῖς. δι' αὐτῆς δὲ τῆς παραινέσεως δείκνυσιν αὐτῶν τὸ ἀκριβὲς τοῦ αλλου βίου.
σπανίως γάρ τις καὶ ἁμαρτάνει καὶ φυσιοῦται· τὸ γὰρ τῆς φυσιώσεως απτεται τῶν
κάλλιστα βιούντων καὶ ὑπ' αὐτοῦ τούτου ὡς τὰ πολλὰ ἐπαιρομένων. Phil 1,7
Πανταχοῦ καὶ διὰ πάντων δείκνυται οὐκ ἀνόνητά μου τὰ παθήματα οὐδὲ αἱ
ἀπολογίαι. ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας πίστεως ἀπόδειξιν ποιοῦμαι τὴν ὑμετέραν ενστασιν.
thought_title: Paul wrote to clergy to instill humility
orientation: Severianus begins his commentary by explaining the audience and purpose of Paul's Letter to the Philippians.
pass_a_gloss: In this letter he writes to clergy, not to laity; for which reason he did not need more of the wrongdoings, but his concern through the letter was that the matter of humility be set right among them. And through the exhortation itself he shows the exactness of their other life. For rarely does someone both sin and become proud; for the matter of pride touches those who live most nobly and who are for the most part lifted up by this very thing. Everywhere and through all things it is shown that my sufferings are not without profit, nor my defenses. From your faith I take a proof, your steadfastness.

choices.why: The genitive plural of ἠδικός refers to ethical or moral topics; rendering as 'moral arguments' fits the context of what Paul did not need more of.
The passive infinitive of κατορθόω means to be brought to a correct state; 'be set right' preserves the passive and the sense of correction.

choices.english: the exactness of their other life
choices.why: ἀκριβές means precision or exactness, and ἄλλου βίου refers to the rest of their conduct; the phrase is kept literal to preserve the argument that their conduct is otherwise precise.
rejected: the strictness of their remaining life
the accuracy of their other way of life

choices.why: The middle/passive participle of ἐπαίρω means being raised up or exalted; 'lifted up' preserves the metaphorical sense of being puffed up with pride.
The adjective means unprofitable or useless; 'without profit' keeps the literal sense of gaining nothing.
The phrase means to produce a demonstration or proof; keeping the noun 'proof' preserves the rhetorical force of Paul's argument.

bible_refs.note: Paul's words are introduced by the reference Phil 1,7 in the source.

pass_b_english: In this letter Paul writes to clergy, not laity. For this reason he did not need to mention many wrongdoings. His aim through the letter was for humility to be set right in them. By the exhortation itself he shows the exactness of their other life. For rarely does someone both sin and become proud. Pride touches those who live most nobly and who, for this very reason, are usually lifted up.
Everywhere and through all things Paul shows that his sufferings and his defenses are not without profit. From your faith I make proof of your steadfastness.

problems.quote: He says, "From your faith I make a proof of your steadfastness."
problems.source_quote: Πανταχοῦ καὶ διὰ πάντων δείκνυται... ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας πίστεως ἀπόδειξιν ποιοῦμαι τὴν ὑμετέραν ἔνστασιν
problems.why: The quotation marks make this Paul's direct speech, but the Greek shows Severianus paraphrasing Paul in third person ('shows... I make' is inconsistent; actually ἀπόδειξιν ποιοῦμαι is Paul's voice quoted).
problems.fix: From your faith I make proof of your steadfastness.
problems.ruling: Greek mixes 3rd-person δείκνυται with 1st-person ποιοῦμαι; quotation marks mislead by attributing all to Paul's direct speech.

edits.old: He says, "From your faith I make a proof of your steadfastness."
edits.new: From your faith I make proof of your steadfastness.

fixed: Removed quotation marks and 'He says' to reflect that the Greek presents Paul's words as quoted proof, not as Severianus's third-person paraphrase.

problems.quote: For this reason he did not need many moral arguments.
problems.why: Source says he did not need many wronged parties, not moral arguments; the glossary term 'clergy/laity' context is lost.
problems.fix: For this reason he did not need to appeal to many who were wronged.
problems.ruling: ἠδικῶν = 'wronged persons' (from ἀδικέω), not 'moral arguments'; meaning completely changed.

problems.quote: For this reason he did not need many moral arguments
problems.source_quote: δι' οπερ οὐδὲ πλειόνων ἐδεήθη ἠδικῶν
problems.why: ἠδικῶν means 'wrongdoings' not 'moral arguments'; sense is 'he did not need many wrongdoings' i.e. Paul didn't need to list many sins
problems.fix: For this reason he did not need to mention many wrongdoings
problems.ruling: ἠδικῶν means 'wrongdoings/offenses'; 'moral arguments' mistranslates, changing the meaning entirely.

edits.old: For this reason he did not need many moral arguments.
edits.new: For this reason he did not need to mention many wrongdoings.

fixed: The omission and glossary problems both concern the same phrase; the English now says he did not need to mention many wrongdoings, matching the source.

problems.quote: I make proof of your steadfastness
problems.why: Same construction varies: 'make proof of,' 'from,' mixing 'faith' and 'steadfastness' as sources.
problems.fix: Standardize preposition and clarify whether faith/steadfastness are synonyms here.

variants.text: I make proof of your steadfastness
I do so from your steadfastness
I do so from your faith

problems.quote: From your faith I make proof of your steadfastness
problems.why: Not exact quotation of Philippians 1:7; conflates elements of 1:7 and 1:25 or 2:12.
problems.fix: Note this is paraphrase combining multiple verses, not direct citation.

edits.old: From your faith I make proof of your steadfastness.
edits.new: From your faith I take proof of your steadfastness.

fixed: The English already says what the source says; the construction is a paraphrase of Philippians 1:7, not a direct quotation, so no change is needed for the scripture issue.
The glossary issue is resolved by using 'take proof' to match the source's 'ἀπόδειξιν ποιοῦμαι' more naturally.

problems.quote: By the exhortation itself he shows the exactness of their other life.
problems.why: 'Exactness of their other life' is opaque; 'other' seems to mean 'rest of' or 'ordinary'.
problems.fix: Clarify as 'the correctness of their everyday life' or 'moral precision in their conduct'.

edits.old: By the exhortation itself he shows the exactness of their other life.
edits.new: By the exhortation itself he shows the moral precision of their conduct.

last_rejected.quote: From your faith I make proof of your steadfastness.
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀπὸ τῆς ὑμετέρας πίστεως ἀπόδειξιν ποιοῦμαι τὴν ὑμετέραν ἔνστασιν.
last_rejected.why: First person 'I make' hides that Paul is speaking, not Severianus.
last_rejected.fix: From your faith he makes proof of your steadfastness.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek first person ποιοῦμαι is Paul's own words quoted by Severianus; 'I make' correctly renders the source voice.

last_rejected.why: Glossary requires 'pride' for φυσίωσις; 'become proud' uses banned paraphrase.
last_rejected.ruling: φυσιοῦται means 'become proud/inflated'; 'become proud' is standard rendering, not a problematic paraphrase.
